segments.name: Alexandria, the City That Names Him

stops.name: Alexandria, the byname and nothing under it
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. No ancient source gives Bathyllus a birth year, a family, a legal status at birth, or a quarter of the city. The single warrant for Alexandria is the byname carried in Athenaeus, Deipnosophistae 1.20d, Bathyllus of Alexandria. The modern estimate of a birth around the middle of the first century BCE is counted backward from his floruit in the 20s and is not an ancient date; the year here orders the segment only. Canonical Alexandria pin, inherited byte-identical from strabo.journey.json and julius_caesar.journey.json.
stops.campa: A man is born in Alexandria and the city keeps his surname for him. Everything else the record gives up. No year, no parents, no street, no word on whether he is born free. What survives is a formula in a Greek compiler working two hundred years later: Bathyllus of Alexandria. It fixes him to Ptolemaic Egypt and to nothing finer than that. Modern books supply a birth around the middle of the first century BCE. The figure is counted backward from the years in which he is famous; no ancient source gives a year at all.
suggested_refs: Athenaeus, Deipnosophistae 1.20d-e, the sole source for the Alexandrian byname
sources: Athenaeus, Deipnosophistae 1.20d-e (Casaubon numbering), tr. C. B. Gulick, Loeb
strabo.journey.json and julius_caesar.journey.json, for the canonical Alexandria pin

stops.name: Alexandria, the theatre quarter at Kom el-Dikka
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. No ancient source names a teacher, a school, or a year for Bathyllus's formation; the trained body presupposed by Athenaeus and by Crinagoras is the only evidence that a formation happened at all. The pin marks Kom el-Dikka, Alexandria's excavated theatre district, at 31.1967, 29.9056; an earlier working coordinate roughly two hundred metres south has been corrected here. The surviving auditorium on the site is fourth century CE and stayed in use into the early seventh, so it postdates him by some four hundred years and marks a district, not a building he ever entered. Date arbitrary.
stops.campa: Greek Alexandria trains performers the way it trains grammarians, by drill. A dancer learns cheironomia, the discipline of the speaking hand, and learns to carry a myth through a mask that cannot change its face. He learns which gods and heroes an audience will recognise from a shoulder. Nothing in the record says who teaches Bathyllus any of it, or where, or at what age. The skill is attested backwards, from the finished man in Rome, and the city gets the credit only because it gets his name. Under the modern street the excavated theatre here was built four centuries after he left.
suggested_refs: The Kom el-Dikka theatre and auditorium complex, Alexandria, fourth to seventh century CE
sources: Athenaeus, Deipnosophistae 1.20d-e
Crinagoras of Mytilene, Greek Anthology 9.542
Wikipedia, 'Kom El Deka', for the corrected coordinate and the fourth-century date of the theatre

stops.name: Alexandria, the Serapeum precinct and the satyr dance
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, and openly inferential. No ancient source places Bathyllus at the Serapeum or at any Alexandrian cult site whatever. The link runs only through the sikinnis, the satyric dance form Athenaeus lists among the three Greek dances he and Pylades combined, and through the Dionysiac performance culture of Ptolemaic Egypt. The coordinate is corrected to 31.1825, 29.8964, the Serapeum plateau at Pompey's Pillar; an earlier working value sat some 1.7 km north in the modern city centre. Date arbitrary.
stops.campa: The sikinnis is the satyrs' dance, a rout, all knees and jolted rhythm, and it belongs to Dionysus wherever Greeks keep his festivals. Ptolemaic Alexandria keeps them on a scale no other city matches. Whether the boy from Alexandria first learns the step on a precinct floor here, or in a private house, or from a hired man in a rented room, no writer says. What is known is that the form ends up in his hands and stays there, and that a Roman satirist eighty years later will name a piece after it and expect his readers to know which piece he means.
suggested_refs: The Serapeum precinct of Alexandria, at the column later called Pompey's Pillar
sources: Athenaeus, Deipnosophistae 1.20d-e, for the sikinnis among the three combined forms
Persius, Satires 5.122-123, for the later fame of the Satyr

stops.name: Memphis, a word whose grammar is disputed
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. Athenaeus 1.20d, citing Seleucus, says Bathyllus was the first to introduce tragic dancing in the style of Memphis. The construction and sense of the Memphite phrase are disputed among modern editors, and no source narrates any journey by Bathyllus to Memphis or anywhere in the Egyptian interior. The pin marks the ancient site at Mit Rahina and records a word in a text, not a visit. Date arbitrary.
stops.campa: Two hundred years after the fact, a compiler reaches for an earlier scholar named Seleucus and writes down that this dancer brought in tragic dancing in the style of Memphis. Then he moves on. Nobody since has agreed on what the phrase attaches to, or whether the style is a genre, a rhythm, a mask, or a place. Memphis lies a hundred and twenty miles up the river from Alexandria, older than Greek Egypt by two thousand years and still working. That phrase is the only thing in the whole record that puts the dancer's name and that city in one line. Whether anything in it points to a journey up the river is a question the record leaves open.
suggested_refs: The ancient site of Memphis at Mit Rahina, Egypt
sources: Athenaeus, Deipnosophistae 1.20d, citing Seleucus, tr. C. B. Gulick, Loeb

stops.name: Alexandria, the Great Harbour
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. No ancient source records Bathyllus leaving Egypt, by any route, in any year. The departure is inferred entirely from his documented Alexandrian byname on one side and his documented presence at Rome on the other. Date arbitrary.
stops.campa: The Portus Magnus takes grain ships all year and passenger traffic when the season allows. From the mole the Pharos stands over the whole roadstead, and Rome eats out of this harbour. Somewhere in the years after Actium a man who will be famous in Latin gets aboard, and no writer of any language notes the day, the ship, the fare, or whether he is travelling as a passenger or as property in someone's baggage. The gap sits between his Alexandrian byname in Athenaeus and his Roman career in everybody else. Nothing fills it.
suggested_refs: The Portus Magnus of Alexandria and the Pharos, the Egyptian end of the Rome grain route
sources: Athenaeus, Deipnosophistae 1.20d-e, for the Alexandrian origin from which the crossing is inferred

stops.name: Puteoli, the Alexandrian landfall
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. No ancient text places Bathyllus at Puteoli or anywhere on the Bay of Naples. The stop follows the well-documented standard route of Alexandrian shipping into Italy in this period and is offered as the most probable landfall, not as testimony about him. Date arbitrary.
stops.campa: Alexandrian ships come into Italy at Puteoli, and the town knows their topsails before it can read their names. The moles run out into the bay, and the Egyptian run is the whole business of the place. No ancient text puts Bathyllus here, or anywhere on the Bay of Naples; the route is documented and the passenger is not. Whoever crosses from Egypt in these decades most likely steps ashore on this quay, among sacks, customs men, and the standing crowd that turns out for every Alexandrian arrival.
suggested_refs: The harbour moles of Puteoli, principal Italian terminus of the Alexandrian run
sources: Inference from the standard Alexandria-to-Italy shipping route; no ancient source names Bathyllus here

stops.name: Ostia, the mouth of the Tiber
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, wholly inferential. No ancient text mentions Bathyllus at Ostia. The stop marks the last leg of a journey that is itself unattested. Date arbitrary.
stops.campa: The last fifteen miles run up a brown river between warehouses. Ostia is where cargo changes from sea hull to barge, and where anyone coming to Rome by water finally sees the city upstream as a smudge of smoke. No source puts Bathyllus on that water. He is in Alexandria in one sentence of Athenaeus and in Rome in every other sentence anyone writes about him, and the ground between is crossed here, or somewhere very like here, in a year nobody wrote down. Upriver the barges go against the current, hauled from the bank.
suggested_refs: Ostia at the Tiber mouth, before Claudius rebuilt the harbour
sources: Inference from general Roman shipping practice; no ancient source names Bathyllus here

stops.name: Rome, the gardens of Maecenas
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, and the tag matters here. The enslavement-and-manumission sequence is modern scholarly reconstruction, not attested. Tacitus, Annals 1.54, says only that Maecenas had fallen violently in love with Bathyllus. Cassius Dio 54.17.5 says only that he was a favourite of Maecenas. Neither states that he entered the household as a slave, and neither mentions manumission. No date, place, or legal instrument survives for either event. Pin inherited from virgil.journey.json, the atlas's Esquiline gardens; the estate is documented, a residence for Bathyllus within it is not. Date arbitrary.
stops.campa: Gaius Cilnius Maecenas handles for Octavian everything that is not war, and keeps gardens on the Esquiline laid over the old burial pits. Into that household comes the dancer from Alexandria. Later scholarship tells the sequence cleanly: bought, owned, freed, kept. The ancient texts do not tell it at all. Tacitus gives the love and Dio gives the favour, and between them there is no bill of sale, no manumission, no witness, and no year. What both authors assume without narrating is that by the time anyone is writing, the tie already exists and everyone in Rome knows it.
suggested_refs: The horti Maecenatis on the Esquiline, over the puticuli
sources: Tacitus, Annals 1.54
Cassius Dio, Roman History 54.17.5
virgil.journey.json, for the canonical Esquiline pin

stops.name: Rome, effusus in amorem Bathylli
stops.date_confidence: Attested, undated. Tacitus, Annals 1.54, written under Trajan and looking back across a century, states the relation as the reason Augustus indulged theatrical shows. Tacitus gives no year for the love and no scene for it; the date orders the segment only. The judgement that Augustus tolerated the dancers' feuds out of complaisance to Maecenas is Tacitus's own analysis of a period he did not live in.
stops.campa: The most powerful private man in Rome is in love with a dancer, and the emperor arranges his cultural policy around it. That is Tacitus's account, set down more than a hundred years afterwards in a single subordinate clause, and it is the only ancient statement of what the two men were to each other. The theatres are watched; performers are whipped and banished at a praetor's word. Whatever Bathyllus is at law by this point, he stands inside the protection of the man who handles Rome for Octavian.
stops.quote: Augustus had countenanced these theatrical exhibitions in complaisance to Maecenas, who had fallen violently in love with Bathyllus.
stops.quote_source: Tacitus, Annals 1.54, tr. John Jackson, Loeb Classical Library (1931)
suggested_refs: Tacitus, Annals 1.54, the sole ancient statement of the relation
sources: Tacitus, Annals 1.54, tr. John Jackson, Loeb, fetched at penelope.uchicago.edu

stops.name: Rome, the auditorium on the Esquiline
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The decorated semi-subterranean hall at Largo Leopardi, conventionally called the Auditorium of Maecenas, is a real structure within the estate, fitted for banqueting and recitation. No ancient source places Bathyllus in it. T. P. Wiseman's proposals in 'Maecenas and the Stage', Papers of the British School at Rome 84 (2016), that Bathyllus danced Cupid, Omphale, or Ganymede in this household, are reconstructions from the anonymous Elegia in Maecenatem and are presented as such. Date arbitrary.
stops.campa: A stepped hall goes down into the Esquiline, painted with garden scenes, cool in August, sized for a company rather than a crowd. Whatever is performed here is performed for a room that already knows everybody in it. A modern reading of the household puts Bathyllus on that floor doing Cupid, or Omphale, or Ganymede, mythic parts for a private audience, and Wiseman says outright that he is reconstructing from the Elegia in Maecenatem. The building stands and is excavated. Nothing ancient names a piece, a night, or a guest.
suggested_refs: The so-called Auditorium of Maecenas, Largo Leopardi, Rome
T. P. Wiseman, 'Maecenas and the Stage', PBSR 84 (2016)
sources: T. P. Wiseman, 'Maecenas and the Stage', PBSR 84 (2016)
The anonymous Elegia in Maecenatem, as read by Wiseman

stops.name: Rome, a name out of the poets
stops.date_confidence: Interpretive, and the underlying facts are separately secure. That Anacreon of Teos loved a Samian boy called Bathyllus, and that Horace recalls the pair, are attested; Horace, Epodes 14.9-10. That imperial pantomimes bore names lifted from the poets is a modern observation, not an ancient remark. No source says whether the dancer was given the name at birth or took it when he began to work. The Samian Bathyllus predates the Alexandrian by roughly five centuries and the two are not the same person. Date arbitrary. Canonical Rome pin, inherited byte-identical from virgil.journey.json.
stops.campa: The name is secondhand. Five hundred years before Augustus, Anacreon of Teos loved a boy of Samos called Bathyllus and made him famous in Greek; Horace, writing in Rome in these same decades, still reaches for the pair when he wants an image of a poet undone by love. Then a dancer from Alexandria carries the name onto a Roman stage and the crowd learns to shout it. Later readers keep the two men in one file across five centuries of distance. Whether his parents gave him the name or he took it off a scroll when he began to work, no writer says.
suggested_refs: Horace, Epodes 14.9-10, on Anacreon and the Samian Bathyllus
sources: Horace, Epodes 14.9-10
Athenaeus, Deipnosophistae 1.20d-e
virgil.journey.json, for the canonical Rome pin

stops.name: Rome, the name that may not be his
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, and a contested one. The epigraphic proposal that Bathyllus's civil name was Gaius Theoros rests on CIL VI 10115 = ILS 5197, in which a dancer named Theoros lists the rivals he defeated and does not list Bathyllus, and on a separate stone describing a female performer, Sophe, with the compound epithet Theorobathylliana. No inscription equates the two names. The Latin epigraphic texts were not pulled directly in this pass and the identification remains unresolved in the literature. Date arbitrary. Canonical Rome pin.
stops.campa: A pantomime called Theoros pays for a stone that names the four men he beat: Pylades of Cilicia, Nomius of Syria, Pierus of Tibur, Hylas of Salmacis. Bathyllus is not on it. One reading of that silence is that the greatest of them was never beaten. Another is that Theoros is Bathyllus, cutting his own civil name over his stage rivals, which would explain a second stone where a dancer named Sophe is called Theorobathylliana, as though the two words were one lineage. No inscription ever sets the names equal. The proposal has stood unresolved for a century.
suggested_refs: CIL VI 10115 = ILS 5197, the victory list of the pantomime Theoros
The inscription of Sophe, described as Theorobathylliana
sources: CIL VI 10115 / ILS 5197, via secondary discussion; epigraphic text not fetched directly

stops.name: Rome, Campus Martius: what the dancer does not do
stops.date_confidence: Attested as an art form, undated as a scene. The division of labour, silent masked dancer against sung and piped narrative, is stated in the chronicle tradition under 22 BCE and is presupposed by Crinagoras, Greek Anthology 9.542, and by Athenaeus. No ancient writer describes how Bathyllus in particular moved. The date orders the segment; the pin marks the Campus Martius theatre quarter and is not an attested location for anything he did.
stops.campa: One dancer, masked, takes every part. A singer or a chorus carries the words, pipes and the scabellum keep the time, and the man on the floor changes person by changing shape. The mask has no working mouth, so the hands do the speaking, and Roman audiences train themselves to read hands the way other audiences read faces. It is a fine enough instrument that two men can fight in public over the meaning of one gesture. Not one ancient writer describes Bathyllus's own handling of it. What survives is the instrument, and the fact that he is credited with building it.
suggested_refs: The Augustan theatre quarter of the Campus Martius
sources: Jerome, Chronicle, Olympiad 189.3 (22 BCE)
Crinagoras, Greek Anthology 9.542
Athenaeus, Deipnosophistae 1.20d-e

stops.name: Rome, Campus Martius: the games for a dead nephew
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, and a modern one. Some scholarship places the public establishment of the new solo pantomime at Rome in 23 BCE, tied to games for Marcellus, Augustus's nephew, who died that year. Marcellus's death in 23 BCE is independently secure. No ancient source connects Bathyllus, or Pylades, or the new form, to his funeral games; the connection is a hypothesis and is not attested. It also sits a year earlier than the only ancient date on record, Jerome's 22 BCE. Venue and year are both contested.
stops.campa: Marcellus dies at nineteen and Rome is given games. A line of modern reconstruction puts the public launch of the new dance there, in the crowd and the mourning of that autumn, one year ahead of Jerome's 22 BCE and with the same two men on the programme. It is an attractive placement. No ancient writer connects Bathyllus, or Pylades, or the new form to the funeral of Marcellus, and no source names a venue for it either. What is certain of that year is the death.
suggested_refs: The funeral games of Marcellus, 23 BCE, and the modern hypothesis attaching the pantomime debut to them
sources: Modern scholarly reconstruction; not attested in any ancient source
Jerome, Chronicle, Ol. 189.3, for the competing 22 BCE date

stops.name: Rome, three dances made into one
stops.date_confidence: Attested, undated, and the date field here is a placement only. Athenaeus 1.20e, citing Aristonicus, credits Bathyllus together with Pylades with developing the Italian style of dance out of the comic kordax, the tragic emmeleia and the satyric sikinnis. Athenaeus supplies no year whatever. The single ancient date in this vicinity, Jerome's Olympiad 189.3 = 22 BCE, belongs to a different source that names Pylades alone and never mentions Bathyllus; the two must not be merged into one dated event. Canonical Rome pin.
stops.campa: Three Greek dances are lying about, each tied to a genre that has been dying for two centuries. The kordax is the comic fling, the emmeleia the tragic measure, the sikinnis the satyr rout. Aristonicus, quoted by Athenaeus, says two men take all three apart and build one thing out of the pieces, and the thing is called the Italian dance. The two men are Pylades of Cilicia and Bathyllus of Alexandria, working as colleagues before they work as enemies. The parts are all old; what is new is that they are made to run together in one body. Athenaeus gives no year for any of it.
suggested_refs: Athenaeus, Deipnosophistae 1.20e, citing Aristonicus, on the making of the Italian dance
sources: Athenaeus, Deipnosophistae 1.20e, citing Aristonicus, tr. C. B. Gulick, Loeb, verified at topostext.org

stops.name: Rome, the tragic dancing in the style of Memphis
stops.date_confidence: Attested, and internally contradictory in its own witness. Athenaeus 1.20d, citing Seleucus, makes Bathyllus the first to introduce tragic dancing in the Memphite manner. Athenaeus 1.20e, a few lines later, makes him the lighter of the two dancers, the one who composed a kind of hyporcheme, against Pylades's solemnity. Editors dispute the passage and it is not resolved here. The clean comic-Bathyllus against tragic-Pylades split that modern accounts report is a smoothing of a text that does not read that way. Date arbitrary. Canonical Rome pin.
stops.campa: The same page of Athenaeus says two things about him and does not notice. In one sentence, on Seleucus's authority, Bathyllus is the man who brought tragic dancing to Rome in the manner of Memphis. In the next paragraph he is the jollier of the pair, the composer of a hyporcheme, set against Pylades's gravity. Editors have argued over the sentence since Casaubon and have not settled it. The tidy division everyone repeats, tragedy to Pylades and comedy to Bathyllus, is drawn out of this same passage. Which of its two statements is the error, if either is, remains open.
stops.quote: Now the first to introduce this 'tragic dancing,' as it was called, in the style of Memphis, was Bathyllus of Alexandria, who, as Seleucus says, danced in pantomime.
stops.quote_source: Athenaeus, Deipnosophistae 1.36 (Casaubon 20d), tr. C. B. Gulick, Loeb Classical Library
suggested_refs: The disputed Memphite clause at Athenaeus 1.20d and its editorial history
sources: Athenaeus, Deipnosophistae 1.20d-e, tr. Gulick, verified at topostext.org/work/218

stops.name: Rome, the chronicle that names only the other man
stops.date_confidence: Attested and precisely dated, but not to him. Jerome's Latin continuation of Eusebius records under Olympiad 189.3, Abr. 1995 = 22 BCE, that Pylades of Cilicia was the first to have a chorus and piper perform for him, where previously performers had sung and danced for themselves. The entry names Pylades alone and does not mention Bathyllus at all. It also does not say the dancer performed silently; it says the chorus and piper performed for him. This stop records what the only dated ancient source says, and what it does not.
stops.campa: The one firm date in the whole business belongs to somebody else. Under the third year of the hundred and eighty-ninth Olympiad, Jerome's chronicle enters a reform: Pylades of Cilicia is the first to have a chorus and a piper perform for him, where before this the performers sang and danced for themselves. Twenty-two years before the era. Bathyllus is not in the sentence. Jerome is writing in the 380s CE, copying out and extending Eusebius, and Athenaeus, who does credit both men jointly, gives no year at all.
stops.quote: Pylades of Cilicia, a performer of mimes, was the first to have a chorus and piper to perform for him, when his predecessor had sung and danced for themselves.
stops.quote_source: Jerome, Chronicle, Olympiad 189.3 (22 BCE), Abr. 1995, tr. via attalus.org
suggested_refs: Jerome's Latin continuation of the Chronicle of Eusebius, entry for Olympiad 189.3
sources: Jerome, Chronicle, Ol. 189.3, verified at attalus.org/translate/jerome2.html
Athenaeus, Deipnosophistae 1.20e, for the undated joint attribution

stops.name: Rome, the treatise that belongs to the other man
stops.date_confidence: Attested as an absence. Athenaeus 1.20e attributes a written treatise on dancing to Pylades, not to Bathyllus. No work by Bathyllus survives, and none is attested as ever having existed. A recurring modern error transfers Pylades's treatise to him; the correction is worth stating because it governs what an edition of Bathyllus could ever be, namely editions of the authors who mention him. Date arbitrary. Canonical Rome pin.
stops.campa: Pylades writes a book about dancing. It is lost, but Athenaeus knows it existed and says so in the same breath in which he names the two men as co-makers of the Italian style. Everything of Bathyllus that reaches us reaches us inside other men's sentences. There is no treatise, no letter, no line of his own in any language, and no ancient writer suggests there ever was one. Modern accounts hand him Pylades's book with some regularity. There is no book.
suggested_refs: Peri orcheseos, the lost treatise on dancing, attributed by Athenaeus to Pylades
sources: Athenaeus, Deipnosophistae 1.20e
Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Antiquities, 'Pantomimus'

stops.name: Rome, Philonides writes for four parts
stops.date_confidence: Attested by a contemporary, undated by him. Crinagoras of Mytilene, Greek Anthology 9.542 = Gow-Page 39, carries no internal date, but Crinagoras's own career is independently fixed by embassies to Rome in 48/47 and 45 BCE and to Tarragona in 26/25 BCE, and he is alive to at least 11 CE, which places the epigram plausibly inside Bathyllus's floruit. The venue is not named. The date orders the segment. Canonical Rome pin.
stops.campa: A working production leaves one trace, and it is a poem. Crinagoras of Mytilene tells a singer named Philonides to go ahead and write for four parts or more, because neither his singing nor the motions of Bathyllus's hands will be short of grace. There is the whole machine in one sentence: a composer, a voice carrying the words, and a silent man taking every role in turn. It is written by somebody who could have been in the room. No title, no theatre, no year, and nobody afterwards names another piece Bathyllus danced.
stops.quote: Never fear, Philonides; write a piece composed for four parts or even more; for neither your singing nor the motions of Bathyllus' hands shall be lacking in grace.
stops.quote_source: Crinagoras of Mytilene, Greek Anthology 9.542, tr. W. R. Paton, Loeb Classical Library
suggested_refs: Crinagoras of Mytilene, Greek Anthology 9.542 = Gow-Page 39
sources: Crinagoras, Greek Anthology 9.542, tr. Paton, verified at attalus.org/poetry/crinagoras.html

stops.name: Theatre of Pompey, the jollier of the two
stops.date_confidence: Attested as a characterisation, undated and unlocated. Athenaeus 1.20e contrasts the two dancers directly: Pylades's dancing solemn, expressing passion and variety of character, Bathyllus's more jolly, and Bathyllus the composer of a kind of hyporcheme. Athenaeus names no venue and no occasion. The Theatre of Pompey pin, inherited from hylas.journey.json, marks the only permanent stone theatre standing at Rome in the early 20s BCE and is the atlas's placement, not the source's. Date arbitrary.
stops.campa: Pompey's theatre is the only permanent stone house in Rome until the year Marcellus's is finished, and whatever reaches a general Roman public in these years most likely reaches it here. Athenaeus sets the two dancers side by side in a single line: one solemn, carrying passion and the changes of character; the other jollier, and the maker of something like a hyporcheme, the old choral dance-song. Four words of Greek, and they are the closest thing to a description of Bathyllus in motion that anybody wrote down. Athenaeus names no venue, no occasion, and no piece.
stops.quote: Pylades' dancing was solemn, expressing passion and variety of character, whereas Bathyllus' was more jolly.
stops.quote_source: Athenaeus, Deipnosophistae 1.37 (Casaubon 20e), tr. C. B. Gulick, Loeb Classical Library
suggested_refs: The Theatre of Pompey, Campus Martius, the only permanent stone theatre at Rome before 13 BCE
sources: Athenaeus, Deipnosophistae 1.20e, tr. Gulick, verified at topostext.org
hylas.journey.json, for the Theatre of Pompey pin

stops.name: Rome, far from himself in tragedy
stops.date_confidence: Attested, undated, unlocated. Seneca the Elder, Controversiae 3, praefatio 10, uses the two dancers as a figure for specialisation: each departs far from himself when working outside his own register. The Latin is verified. Seneca names no performance, no year, and no venue, and the passage is a rhetorician's analogy, not a review. Note also that it sits in tension with Athenaeus 1.20d, which makes Bathyllus the introducer of tragic dancing; the contradiction is left standing. Date arbitrary. Canonical Rome pin.
stops.campa: A teacher of rhetoric wants an example of a man working outside his own gift, and reaches for the two most famous bodies in Rome. Pylades in comedy, Bathyllus in tragedy: each of them, says Seneca, departs far from himself. The line only works if his audience has seen both men try, and seen both come off worse. So Bathyllus does take the graver register on occasion, and Rome remembers the attempts as failures. Which role, in which year, before whom? Seneca is teaching declamation, not reviewing performances, and never says.
stops.quote: Pylades in comoedia, Bathyllus in tragoedia multum a se aberrant.
stops.quote_source: Seneca the Elder, Controversiae 3, praefatio 10 (Latin text, thelatinlibrary.com)
suggested_refs: Seneca the Elder, Controversiae 3, praefatio, on specialisation among performers
sources: Seneca the Elder, Controversiae 3 pref. 10, Latin verified at thelatinlibrary.com
Athenaeus, Deipnosophistae 1.20d, for the contradicting tragic attribution

stops.name: Rome, a declamation hall: the boast and its answer
stops.date_confidence: Attested verbatim, undated and unlocated. Seneca the Elder preserves the rhetor Cestius's boast and the reply Cassius Severus gave it; the Latin is verified at la.wikisource.org, Controversiae. Seneca gives no year and does not say where the exchange happened; the declamation hall is unlocated and the pin is the canonical Rome pin. The passage is mockery of Cestius, not a neutral endorsement of Bathyllus, and quoting the boast without the answer misrepresents the source.
stops.campa: Cestius the rhetor, a Greek out of Smyrna teaching Latin declamation, tells a room what he would be in any other trade. If I were a Thracian gladiator, I would be Fusius; if I were a pantomime, I would be Bathyllus; if a horse, Melissio. The list is a list of the best in each line, and the dancer stands in it beside a champion and a racehorse without needing explanation. Cassius Severus, listening, could not hold his bile, and shouted back: if you were a sewer, you would be the Cloaca Maxima.
stops.quote: si Thraex essem, Fusius essem; si pantomimus essem, Bathyllus essem; si equus, Melissio.
stops.quote_source: Cestius, in Seneca the Elder, Controversiae 3, praefatio 16 (Latin verified at la.wikisource.org)
suggested_refs: Seneca the Elder, Controversiae 3 pref. 16, with the reply of Cassius Severus
sources: Seneca the Elder, Controversiae 3 pref. 16, Latin verified at la.wikisource.org

stops.name: Rome, the Satyr
stops.date_confidence: The routine is attested only by its afterlife. Persius, Satires 5.122-123, writing under Nero some eighty years later, names the Satyr of Bathyllus as a byword for demanding choreography and warns a dilettante against attempting even three of its beats. Persius is the sole witness. Nothing survives about when Bathyllus made the piece, where he danced it, what it depicted, or how long it ran; the stop is placed inside his career because the piece is his, and the date is arbitrary. Canonical Rome pin.
stops.campa: There is one named piece, and it comes down to posterity as a warning. Somewhere in these years Bathyllus makes a satyr dance hard enough that a Roman a lifetime later can invoke it as the thing an amateur must not try. What it showed, how long it lasted, which myth it hung on, whether it used the sikinnis he brought out of Egypt, none of that survives. What survives is a name for it and the assumption that the reader knows the name. Persius uses it the way a modern writer would use a famous cadenza: as a measure of how far out of your depth you are.
stops.quote: haec miscere nefas nec, cum sis cetera fossor, / tris tantum ad numeros Satyrum moueare Bathylli.
suggested_refs: Persius, Satires 5.122-123, the sole witness to the Satyr of Bathyllus
sources: Persius, Satires 5.122-123, Latin verified at thelatinlibrary.com

stops.name: Theatre of Pompey, the flute player called Princeps
stops.date_confidence: Attested, undated, unlocated. Phaedrus, Fabulae 5.7, verified at thelatinlibrary.com, opens by saying that a flute player somewhat well known, called Princeps, had been accustomed to give his services to Bathyllus on stage. Phaedrus names no venue, no year, and no piece; the Theatre of Pompey pin is the atlas's own placement and is not evidenced. The rest of the fable, the fall from the stage machinery and the misheard chorus, happens years later under an unnamed emperor and is not part of Bathyllus's own record. Date arbitrary.
stops.campa: Somebody has to play the pipes. Phaedrus, telling a fable about vanity two generations later, needs to establish that his flute player mattered, and does it in half a line: Princeps was fairly well known, and he used to give his services to Bathyllus on the stage. That is the whole of it, thrown away as a credential. The dancer's name is the qualification; nothing further needs saying. Years afterwards the same man breaks his leg falling from the machinery, comes back, and hears a chorus singing for the emperor as applause for himself.
stops.quote: Princeps tibicen notior paulo fuit, / operam Bathyllo solitus in scaena dare.
suggested_refs: Phaedrus, Fabulae 5.7, the fable of the flute player Princeps
sources: Phaedrus, Fabulae 5.7, Latin verified at thelatinlibrary.com

stops.name: Palatine, the emperor rebukes the other man
stops.date_confidence: Attested, and now correctly dated. Cassius Dio 54.17.4-5, verified at penelope.uchicago.edu, has Augustus rebuke Pylades for quarrelling with Bathyllus, a fellow artist and a favourite of Maecenas. Dio 54 carries the consular heading for 19 BCE at chapter 10 and the next, for 17 BCE, at chapter 18, so chapter 17 sits in the narrative for 18 BCE, beside the Julian marriage legislation of chapter 16. Dio reports Pylades's recall from exile first and this exchange after, and does not date the exchange relative to the recall. Dio writes in the early third century CE and no verbatim value attaches to the reply. Palatine pin inherited from virgil.journey.json via hylas.journey.json; Dio names no place.
stops.campa: The feud gets loud enough that the emperor takes an interest, and he takes it in the wrong direction for Bathyllus's rival. Augustus reproaches Pylades for quarrelling with his colleague, and Dio makes a point of identifying the colleague: Bathyllus, a fellow artist, and a favourite of Maecenas. Pylades answers with the line that outlived both of them, that it serves Caesar for the people to spend their idle hours on dancers. Two centuries separate the exchange from the man writing it down. What Bathyllus said, or whether he was in the room, Dio does not report.
stops.quote: It is to your advantage, Caesar, that the people should devote their spare time to us.
stops.quote_source: Pylades to Augustus, Cassius Dio, Roman History 54.17.5, tr. Earnest Cary, Loeb Classical Library
suggested_refs: Cassius Dio, Roman History 54.17.4-5, on the quarrel and the reply
sources: Cassius Dio, Roman History 54.17.4-5, verified at penelope.uchicago.edu
hylas.journey.json, which reads the same passage from the other tradition

stops.name: Rome, the version in which he does not appear
stops.date_confidence: A source conflict, stated and not resolved. Cassius Dio 54.17.4-5 puts Bathyllus opposite Pylades in the quarrel that draws Augustus's rebuke. Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7.19, writing in the early fifth century CE, attaches a reply of the same kind to a rivalry between Pylades and his pupil Hylas, in different words, with Bathyllus absent. The two traditions cannot both be reports of one event and neither is used here to fill the other's gaps; hylas.journey.json reads the same conflict from the other side. Date arbitrary. Canonical Rome pin.
stops.campa: There is a second telling in which Bathyllus is not there at all. Macrobius, four centuries after the quarrel and two after Dio, gives the same shape of story with Pylades's own pupil Hylas standing where Bathyllus stands, and puts different Greek in Pylades's mouth. Modern retellings have merged the two and produced episodes that neither author wrote. Which man was the rival Augustus rebuked, if there was one quarrel and not two, is a question neither text can settle from the other.
suggested_refs: Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7.19, the competing version of the rebuke
sources: Cassius Dio, Roman History 54.17.4-5
Macrobius, Saturnalia 2.7.19, via hylas.journey.json

stops.name: Rome, the expulsion that had another cause
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction where it is usually told as fact. The chain feud with Bathyllus, therefore expulsion, is attested by neither source. Suetonius, Divus Augustus 45, verified, attributes Pylades's expulsion from Rome and from Italy to his pointing out a hissing spectator and turning the crowd on him; Bathyllus is not mentioned. Dio 54.17.4, verified, attributes an earlier exile to sedition, also without mentioning Bathyllus, and reports the Bathyllus quarrel only as the occasion of a verbal rebuke, not of banishment. The two accounts may describe different episodes entirely. Date arbitrary. Canonical Rome pin.
stops.campa: Pylades is thrown out of Rome and out of Italy. Every popular account attaches that to the feud; no ancient source does. Dio mentions an earlier exile for sedition and never brings Bathyllus into it, and the two accounts may not even be about the same episode. Suetonius gives the cause as a finger: the dancer picks a hissing spectator out of the benches and points, the whole house turns on the man, and the emperor will not have a performer directing a crowd from the floor.
suggested_refs: Suetonius, Divus Augustus 45, on the expulsion of Pylades
sources: Suetonius, Divus Augustus 45, verified at penelope.uchicago.edu
Cassius Dio, Roman History 54.17.4

stops.name: Rome, no punishment on his side of the record
stops.date_confidence: A documented asymmetry, stated as such. Suetonius, Divus Augustus 45, records three punishments in one breath: Hylas flogged in the atrium of his own house on a praetor's complaint, the actor Stephanio whipped through all three theatres and banished, Pylades expelled from Rome and Italy. No ancient source records any punishment, exile, fine, or reprimand of Bathyllus, ever. That is an absence in the evidence, not proof that he was never disciplined. Date arbitrary. Canonical Rome pin.
stops.campa: Augustus keeps a list and works down it. Stephanio is whipped through all three theatres and sent away. Hylas is flogged in the atrium of his own house with the doors open, because a praetor complained. Pylades is put out of Italy. Suetonius sets the three side by side without saying they are connected, and Bathyllus is on none of the lines. No source anywhere records a punishment of him, of any kind, at any point. He is also the one of the four with Maecenas standing behind him. That is an absence in the evidence and nothing more.
suggested_refs: Suetonius, Divus Augustus 45.4, the three punishments in one passage
sources: Suetonius, Divus Augustus 45, verified at penelope.uchicago.edu

segments.name: The House That Stands Through Successors

stops.name: Theatre of Marcellus, the second stone house
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction as to Bathyllus, attested as to the building. The Theatre of Marcellus was completed in 13 BCE and formally inaugurated by Augustus in 12 BCE. No ancient source places Bathyllus in it or at its opening. The stop marks the era's major new venue during what is plausibly the tail of his working life, since Maecenas is still alive; nothing more should be read into it. Pin inherited from hylas.journey.json; an earlier working coordinate some three hundred metres southeast has been corrected.
stops.campa: Rome gets its second permanent theatre, named for the dead nephew whose games one line of scholarship makes the debut of the whole new form. It is finished in 13 and Augustus opens it in 12, and from then on the Italian dance has two stone houses to fill instead of one. Whether Bathyllus is still working, still alive, or already gone by the year the scaffolding comes down, no source says. Maecenas is alive in these years. Nothing else in the record touches them.
suggested_refs: The Theatre of Marcellus, completed 13 BCE, inaugurated 12 BCE
sources: Wikipedia, 'Theatre of Marcellus', for the corrected coordinate and the 13/12 BCE dates
hylas.journey.json, for the atlas pin

stops.name: Rome, the Esquiline: Maecenas dies
stops.date_confidence: The death is secure; the connection to Bathyllus is a gap. Maecenas dies in 8 BCE, a date widely and independently attested in the ancient tradition. No ancient source states whether Bathyllus was alive at that point, present, named in the will, provided for, or affected in any way. His absence from every account of the death and its aftermath is a documented silence and is recorded here as one, not filled.
stops.campa: Maecenas dies in his sixties and leaves his fortune to Augustus. The gardens on the Esquiline pass to the emperor; the household that stood between one Alexandrian dancer and the whole apparatus of Roman discipline stops existing as a household. Whether Bathyllus is standing in the room, or dead already, or old, or somewhere else entirely, is not recorded by anyone. He is not in the will as anyone reports it. He is not in the funeral. Nobody who writes about the death of Maecenas writes about him.
suggested_refs: The death of Maecenas, 8 BCE, and the passage of the horti to Augustus
sources: Ancient consensus on Maecenas's death in 8 BCE
No ancient source connects Bathyllus to the event; recorded as a gap

stops.name: Rome, no death, no tomb, no will
stops.date_confidence: A gap, confirmed rather than asserted. No ancient source records the date, place, cause, or circumstances of Bathyllus's death, nor any retirement, final performance, illness, testament, or disposition of property. The absence holds across every primary text checked: Athenaeus, Tacitus, Dio, Suetonius, Persius, Phaedrus, both Senecas and Crinagoras, and across Smith's Dictionary and the standard modern summaries. The only ancient stone anywhere bearing the name commemorates a different man; see suggested_refs. Date arbitrary and marks the end of the traceable record, not an event.
stops.campa: The record simply stops. There is no death year, no cause, no city, no grave, no last performance, no will, no property, no heir, no epitaph, and no ancient writer who thought any of that worth a line. A grave stele at Verona does carry the name, cut for a youth of an Athenian theatrical family called Gaius Silius Bathyllus, dead in the middle of the second century CE, and specialists list him as a third man of the name. He is not this one. No authenticated portrait or monument of the Alexandrian is known to exist.
suggested_refs: The grave stele of Gaius Silius Bathyllus, Museo Lapidario Maffei, Verona, mid-second century CE, commemorating a different man of the same name
sources: theatrum.de/2241.html, distinguishing Bathyllus I, II and III
Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Antiquities, 'Pantomimus'
en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bathyllus

stops.name: Rome, the theatres riot without him
stops.date_confidence: Attested and dated, but not about him. Tacitus, Annals 1.54, records disorder among rival pantomime factions at the first Augustalia after Augustus's death in 14 CE; Annals 1.77 records a worse riot in 15 CE in which members of the public, several soldiers and a centurion were killed and a Praetorian officer wounded, prompting the Senate to bar senators from actors' houses and knights from escorting performers. No source places Bathyllus at either. His presence, survival, or involvement is unattested in both directions. Canonical Rome pin.
stops.campa: Thirty years on, the thing the two dancers built is killing people. At the first Augustalia after Augustus is dead the factions fight in the theatre; the year after, the fighting takes several of the public, several soldiers, and a centurion, and wounds an officer of the Praetorian Guard. The Senate responds by forbidding senators to enter actors' houses and knights to walk with performers in the street. It is the same partisanship the two dancers made their careers on, thirty years further along. Whether the man from Alexandria is alive to hear about any of it, nothing says.
suggested_refs: Tacitus, Annals 1.54 and 1.77, on the theatrical factions of 14 and 15 CE
sources: Tacitus, Annals 1.54 and 1.77, verified at penelope.uchicago.edu

stops.name: Rome, stat per successores
stops.date_confidence: Attested in the Latin. Seneca the Younger, Naturales Quaestiones 7.32.3, composed in the early to mid 60s CE, verified at thelatinlibrary.com. The Latin quoted here is primary; the English gloss widely quoted in the literature could not be matched to any published translation and is not used. Domus can mean house, lineage, or school, and Seneca does not disambiguate. The passage documents institutional succession under the name, not that Bathyllus was alive. The date is the approximate composition date, not an event in his life. Canonical Rome pin.
stops.campa: Seneca is complaining that the philosophical schools have died out while nobody lets a pantomime's name drop. Then he says the thing that turns out to be the whole afterlife: the house of Pylades and Bathyllus stands through successors, these arts have many pupils and many teachers, and all over the city the private stage is sounding. Eighty years after the quarrel the two names are institutions. His word for it is domus, which will not decide between a building, a bloodline, and a technique passed hand to hand. He is not praising them. He is using them to shame the philosophers.
stops.quote: Stat per successores Pyladis et Bathylli domus, harum artium multi discipuli sunt multique doctores; priuatum urbe tota sonat pulpitum.
stops.quote_source: Seneca the Younger, Naturales Quaestiones 7.32.3 (Latin, thelatinlibrary.com)
suggested_refs: Seneca the Younger, Naturales Quaestiones 7.32.3, on the surviving schools of the two dancers
sources: Seneca, Naturales Quaestiones 7.32.3, Latin verified at thelatinlibrary.com/sen/sen.qn7.shtml

stops.name: Rome, the Leda and the matrons
stops.date_confidence: Attested text, contested identification. Juvenal, Satires 6.60-65, describes a dancer named Bathyllus performing Leda and reducing Roman women in the audience to open sexual frenzy. Juvenal writes roughly a century after the Augustan floruit and does not say which Bathyllus he means. The argument that this is a later performer using the same famous stage name, or a stylised generic reference, is scholarly interpretation and is not stated by Juvenal. The date is Juvenal's approximate composition period, not an event in the Alexandrian's life. Canonical Rome pin.
stops.campa: A century later the name is still on a Roman stage and still means the same thing, a body doing a myth. Juvenal has a Bathyllus dance Leda, and the women in the seats lose their composure and their continence in ways he itemises for the pleasure of itemising them. Juvenal is writing at the audience, and the dancer is his instrument for getting at them. Whether this is a successor working under the founder's name, a stylised figure, or Juvenal simply reaching for the most famous dancer's name in Latin, he never says and nobody has settled it since.
stops.quote: When sinuous Bathyllus dances his pantomime Leda, Tucia loses control of her bladder, and Apula yelps
stops.quote_source: Juvenal, Satires 6.60-63, tr. A. S. Kline, poetryintranslation.com
suggested_refs: Juvenal, Satires 6.60-65, on a dancer named Bathyllus performing Leda
sources: Juvenal, Satires 6.60-63, tr. Kline, fetched at poetryintranslation.com
en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bathyllus, for the disputed identification

stops.name: Rome, the poet who did not write the couplet
stops.date_confidence: Legend, late, and explicitly not biography. The expanded Vita Vergilii of the Donatus auctus tradition tells of an inferior poet named Bathyllus who claimed credit for anonymous verses honouring Augustus that Virgil had written, and was exposed when Virgil completed the line with sic vos non vobis. The text is a medieval expansion of uncertain date; 500 CE is an ordering placement only. No source naming the dancer describes him as a poet, and the identification of this Bathyllus with Maecenas's dancer is unsupported. It is recorded here as a named legend, not resolved and not endorsed. Canonical Rome pin.
stops.campa: A story attaches itself, centuries later, to the wrong man. In the expanded life of Virgil a poet called Bathyllus takes the credit for anonymous verses praising Augustus, and Virgil exposes him by starting a line four times over and finishing it: so you, but not for yourselves. The tale is late, the manuscript tradition that carries it is an expansion of an expansion, and nothing that names the dancer ever calls him a writer. Popular accounts fold the two Bathylli together anyway; virgil.journey.json runs on the earlier tradition, where the episode does not appear.
suggested_refs: The Donatus auctus expansion of the Vita Vergilii and the sic vos non vobis anecdote
sources: The expanded Vita Vergilii tradition, summarised at virgil.org/vitae/; Latin text not fetched
virgil.journey.json, which does not carry the anecdote

stops.name: Paris, Le Mime Bathylle
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Jean Bertheroy, pen name of Berthe-Corinne Le Barillier (1858-1927), published the historical novel Le Mime Bathylle in 1894, listed on fr.wikisource.org as roman historique suivi de Alounea. The year and the pairing with Alounea are confirmed on that page. A publisher attribution to Armand Colin circulates but does not appear there and is not carried here. The work is fiction and is not evidence about the dancer.
stops.campa: Nineteen centuries after the last ancient sentence about him, a French novelist writing as Jean Bertheroy gives Bathyllus a plot. Le Mime Bathylle appears in 1894, bound with a second tale called Alounea, and it is a novel, which is to say it supplies everything the record refuses: motive, dialogue, an interior. Bertheroy is Berthe-Corinne Le Barillier, born in 1858 and dead in 1927, working in the late-century French appetite for a decadent and sensuous antiquity. None of it is evidence about the dancer, and none of it claims to be.
suggested_refs: Jean Bertheroy, Le Mime Bathylle, roman historique suivi de Alounea (1894)
sources: fr.wikisource.org/wiki/Auteur:Jean_Bertheroy, fetched directly

stops.name: Hanover, New Hampshire, Bathyllus in the Swan Dance
stops.date_confidence: Attested, with corrections. The Hood Museum of Art at Dartmouth College holds accession PR.917.12.3, Aubrey Vincent Beardsley (1872-1898), full title 'Bathyllus in the Swan Dance (Unpublished illustration for The Sixth Satire of Juvenal)'. The museum records it as a line-block print on paper, not a pen-and-ink drawing, and dates it circa 1896, not firmly 1896. Its subject is Juvenal's dancer, whose identity with the Augustan Bathyllus is itself disputed. The pin is the holding institution, not a place the dancer ever stood.
stops.campa: Beardsley draws him for a Juvenal that never gets published. The line-block print carries the title Bathyllus in the Swan Dance, made around 1896, two years before Beardsley is dead at twenty-five, and it belongs to the last stretch of work in which he is illustrating the Sixth Satire for a private edition. The dancer in the picture is Juvenal's, which is to say possibly not the Alexandrian at all. It ends up catalogued in a college museum in New Hampshire under the accession number PR.917.12.3.
suggested_refs: Aubrey Beardsley, 'Bathyllus in the Swan Dance', line-block print, c. 1896, Hood Museum of Art, Dartmouth College, PR.917.12.3
sources: hoodmuseum.dartmouth.edu/objects/pr.917.12.3, fetched directly

stops.name: Rome, the Esquiline read again
stops.date_confidence: Attested as scholarship, dated to publication. T. P. Wiseman, 'Maecenas and the Stage', Papers of the British School at Rome 84 (2016), reconstructs Bathyllus as the virtuoso dancer, the slave, freedman and lover of Maecenas, and one of the greatest stars of the Roman theatre games, and proposes mythological scenarios staged privately in the Esquiline gardens. The reconstruction is careful and is not attestation; the ancient sources say only what they say. The date is the article's, not an event in the dancer's life. Esquiline pin.
stops.campa: The gardens get read again, and the dancer comes back into the argument. Wiseman's paper puts Bathyllus at the centre of what Maecenas's household was actually for, treating the private stage as the point rather than a decoration, and builds from the anonymous Elegia in Maecenatem a case for Dionysiac scenarios and a Hercules and Omphale danced indoors for a small room. Wiseman labels the whole of it reconstruction, built from a fragment and a poem nobody signed. The ancient sources still say only what they say.
suggested_refs: T. P. Wiseman, 'Maecenas and the Stage', Papers of the British School at Rome 84 (2016)
